title: Accordion Batcher — latency-aware hybrid orchestration proposal
content:
Purpose
------
This doc describes the "Accordion Batcher", a hybrid continuous-batching scheduler designed to reduce per-token cost while preserving p95/p99 latency SLOs and providing predictable fairness across clients. The approach tries to get the best of two worlds: request-level batching for large multi-token generations and token-level opportunistic coalescing for short/streaming workloads.

Motivation and problem statement
--------------------------------
- We observe two dominant workload shapes: long continuous generations (LLM-as-batch jobs) that benefit from large GPU kernels and short interactive calls (chat-like) where latency matters.
- Pure token-level coalescing boosts throughput but can increase tail latency for high-priority interactive requests and complicate KV cache locality (mixing contexts hurts cache hits).
- Pure request-level batching minimizes kernel invocation overhead but blocks small requests until batch fills or fixed timers expire.
- We need a unified scheduler that:
  - preserves latency SLOs for latency-sensitive classes,
  - improves utilization for throughput-oriented jobs,
  - avoids harming KV cache hit rates,
  - provides measurable fairness across customers and routes.

High-level idea: Accordion Batcher
----------------------------------
The scheduler organizes time into "elastic microframes" (not fixed windows) and maintains two coordinated queues:
- Priority lanes: per-SLA/request-priority FIFO buckets for latency-sensitive requests.
- Elastic coalescing pool: a dynamic reservoir that accepts token-level fragments from low-priority/throughput workloads.

Key behavioral rules:
1) Low-latency requests bypass the elastic pool by default and are scheduled with strict deadline-aware fast-paths.
2) Throughput requests start in request-mode: they attempt to acquire a full-batch reservation (N tokens or M requests) within a soft timeout. If the request is long (remaining tokens > threshold) it will be split into a head chunk that can be ready for immediate request-level batching and a tail that becomes eligible for token-level coalescing.
3) Short requests (< T_short tokens) may opportunistically join the elastic coalescing pool if latency slack permits, with a bounded join-delay proportional to current utilization and priority.
4) The "accordion" behavior: as load shifts, the scheduler stretches (more token-level coalescing) or compresses (more request-level batching) the coalescing pool capacity. This is governed by utilization, observed latency, and KV cache hit ratio signals.

Fairness model
---------------
We propose a credit-based fairness overlay that operates at two granularities: request-credit and token-credit.
- Each API key / route gets a rolling budget of request-credits and token-credits based on SLA tier and recent usage.
- Request-credits control how often a tenant can take the low-latency fast-path. Token-credits regulate how aggressively a tenant's long jobs can be coalesced into the elastic pool.
- When system contention is high, the scheduler drains token-credits faster for heavy tenants, causing their throughput jobs to see smaller coalesced batches (more kernels invoked) but preserving request-credits for interactive calls.
- Credits decay over a sliding window (e.g., 60s) and are replenished according to configured policies (burst allowances, committed capacity).

KV cache affinity and kernel selection
-------------------------------------
- Core insight: KV cache hits are highly sensitive to mixing multiple request contexts on the same KV shard. Excessive token-level coalescing across clients reduces effective cache hit rates and increases per-token latency.
- Affinity policy: when coalescing, prefer requests that share model-version + user-session + route tag. A soft affinity score is maintained per queued fragment. The elastic pool uses affinity-weighted selection when forming kernel input batches.
- Kernel selection: prefer fused long-sequence kernels for request-mode batches and incremental-attention kernels for token-mode batches. The scheduler exposes expected kernel shape to the kernel selector so we can pick quantization / kernel LUTs accordingly.

Latency SLO handling and fast-paths
----------------------------------
- Deadline tagging: each request carries an effective deadline = now + user_SLO_margin. The scheduler honors deadlines with a preemptive uplift in the priority lanes.
- Fast-path tokens: if a request is within X ms of its deadline, it will be prioritized into the next immediate dispatch even if batch size is below desired throughput target.
- If preemption occurs frequently for a given kernel, the scheduler lowers that kernel's coalescing aggressiveness (reduces accordion stretch) to avoid thrashing.

Admission and backpressure
---------------------------
- New requests are admitted if they have enough credits or if system utilization is below a safe threshold.
- When capacity is constrained, the system can: reroute to cheaper model variants, degrade token-coalescing aggressiveness for low-priority tenants, or reject/expose 429 with retry-after hints.

Implementation sketch
---------------------
Data structures (conceptual):
- PriorityQueue[priority_lane] -> FIFO of requests (request-level entries).
- ElasticPool -> list of token-fragments with affinity tags and timestamps.
- CreditLedger[tenant] -> sliding-window counters for request and token credits.
- KernelPlanner -> maps candidate batches to kernel types and estimated latency/cost.

Scheduler loop (simplified):
1) drain high-priority lanes into immediate dispatch candidates if deadlines approaching.
2) assemble request-mode batches from priority FIFO when batch fullness or timer thresholds hit.
3) fill remaining GPU capacity by pulling affinity-aligned fragments from ElasticPool respecting credits and latency slack.
4) consult KernelPlanner to finalize kernel invocation and serialize batch metadata for KV cache accounting.
5) update credits, metrics, and per-tenant fairness ledgers.

Experimentation plan and metrics
-------------------------------
A/B variants to test:
- V1: baseline continuous token-coalescing (current prod-like).
- V2: Accordion Batcher with permissive affinity and basic credits.
- V3: Accordion Batcher + strict affinity + dynamic accordion tuning.

Metrics to collect (per-tenant and global):
- p50/p95/p99 generation latency, token-level and request-level.
- tokens/sec and GPU utilization by kernel type.
- KV cache hit rate (per-model / per-shard).
- fairness delta: ratio of median latency across tenants in top and bottom deciles.
- billing accuracy and token-count variance.

Open questions and risks
------------------------
- How to pick thresholds for splitting long requests into head/tail chunks without introducing reassembly complexity? (tradeoff: increased RPCs vs better packing)
- Is the credit model intuitive for product teams (billing + SLA mapping)? Might need UX/console controls.
- Kernel fragmentation risk: frequent small kernels could offset coalescing gains. We need a dynamic cost model in KernelPlanner.
- How much state does per-fragment affinity tracking add to the scheduler? Memory/cost tradeoffs.
- Cold-starts: heavy affinity heuristics could harm cold clients who don't have session signals. We should fall back to route+model affinity.

Next steps / TODOs
------------------
- Sync with Priya on KV-shard affinity signals (RI-7891).
- Prototype KernelPlanner mock to estimate cost delta for mixed kernels (Evan).
- Add basic credit ledger + simple UI circuit-breaker to Console for experiments (Benji).
- Run microbench cluster experiments on staging for V2 vs baseline for 48h and collect per-tenant fairness metrics.
- Draft end-to-end PR with simulation harness and lightweight scheduler to iterate quickly: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1423

Notes to reviewers
------------------
- This is intentionally exploratory — looking for feedback on the credit shapes, split heuristics, and whether to prioritize affinity or latency when they conflict.
- If we like this direction, we should plan an internal /confluence doc with policy knobs exposed to SRE and product for rollout controls.

References and related work
--------------------------
- Prior notes: continuous-batcher experiments (see linked PR and Slack).
- Academic: "Dynamic batching for low-latency inference"; "Affinity-aware cache scheduling" (refs in the code PR).

End.
